summary:
We developed a non-invasive autonomous biomedical monitoring system in two phases executed through local embedded processing. To address the challenge of cephalothoracic fluid shift in microgravity, the system employs an optical capture station that processes 30 frames of the astronaut to calculate their height and generate a three-dimensional trisectoral model (frontal, profile, and 3/4 views).
This mesh is periodically contrasted with the pre-flight baseline to identify edema or inflammation in the chest and head. In parallel, a microcontroller module with a MAX30102 heart sensor and OLED screen analyzes heart rate and blood oxygenation in real-time, evaluating nominal readings against risk levels using local algorithms. Upon detecting any biometric variation, the firmware activates an immediate sound alert. If the 3D capture shows data where there has been an increase in certain cubic centimeters expressed as percentages of the thorax or head, then the necessary protocols will be activated.
This solution guaranties critical medical autonomy in deep space missions such as Mars, where there are communication delays with Earth, based on data from NASA's Fluid Shifts study and parameters of the NASA-STD-3001 standard. (Human Systems Standard for Space Flights).
details:
What It Does & How It Works ORBITAL HEALTH (ASTROMEDIC) is a complete medical monitoring system built to track how a person’s body adapts to extreme conditions, like microgravity. To make it truly reliable, we split the hardware into two main parts:

  1. The Wearable Band: The user wears a small band powered by an ESP32-C3 microcontroller and a MAX30102 sensor. It reads heart rate and blood oxygen (SpO2) 400 times per second. Since movement easily ruins optical sensor data, we wrote custom digital filters (median and moving average) to clean the signal. It sends the clean vitals wirelessly every second using ESP-NOW.
  2. The Base Station: This is a second ESP32 with an OLED screen and a buzzer, powered entirely by a portable powerbank. It listens for the wearable's data. If it detects a critical drop in oxygen (under 90%) or dangerous heart rates, it sounds the alarm immediately—even if the main computer crashes or loses power. At the same time, it forwards the data over Wi-Fi to a local server.
  3. The Software & Dashboard: A Python backend runs a clinical Decision Tree to classify the vitals and logs everything into an SQLite database (oxigeno_mision.db). We visualize this on a custom Mission Control web dashboard that combines these live vitals with 16 physical body measurements taken via computer vision (anthropometry), plus the user's daily self-reported symptoms.

Benefits & Intended Impact The biggest benefit of this architecture is that it completely removes single points of failure. By moving away from unstable USB serial connections and letting the base station run on a powerbank, the local medical alarms work no matter what. Also, instead of relying on generic medical averages, the system compares live data against the user's personal baseline (like a specific 74 BPM resting pulse). The goal is to give crews in deep space—or doctors in remote, low-resource clinics on Earth—an affordable, easy-to-understand tool that tells them exactly what's happening to the patient and when they need to act.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software We built the hardware using an ESP32-C3, a standard ESP32, a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, I2C OLED screens, and an active buzzer. The embedded code is written in C++ using the Arduino IDE, relying heavily on the esp_now, WiFi, and U8g2lib libraries. The backend runs on Python 3 with standard SQLite for the database. For the frontend, we skipped heavy frameworks and built a fast, custom dashboard using HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript, featuring live SVG charting.

How the Project Is Creative & Factors Considered What makes this project unique is how we cross-reference different types of data. We aren't just looking at a heart rate monitor; we correlate the cardiovascular data with physical body changes (using Z-scores for 16 body segments)to tell the difference between a normal workout and a real fluid-shift issue caused by microgravity. During development, our main challenge was signal noise, so we spent a lot of time tweaking the IR threshold gating and smoothing algorithms. We also implemented a "3-packet confirmation" rule for the buzzer: the alarm only goes off if it receives three consecutive bad readings, completely avoiding false alarms from a momentary sensor slip.
